question: Two resistors of 15 Omega and 5 Omega are connected in series with a 12 V battery. How much current will flow in the circuit?
solution:
The correct answer is __**0.6 A**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **total resistance** in a series circuit is the sum of the individual resistances. In this case, the two resistors are **15 Ω** and **5 Ω**, so the total resistance is:

 **R_total = R1 + R2 = 15 Ω + 5 Ω = 20 Ω**.
 
• The circuit is powered by a **12 V battery**, and the current in a series circuit can be calculated using **Ohm's Law**, which states:

 **I = V / R**, where:
 
 
• **I** is the current,
 
• **V** is the voltage, and
 
• **R** is the total resistance.
 
 Substituting the values: **I = 12 V / 20 Ω = 0.6 A**.
 
• In a series circuit, the current remains **constant** throughout all components. Hence, the current flowing through both the **15 Ω resistor** and the **5 Ω resistor** is **0.6 A**.
 
• The resistors' purpose in the circuit is to limit the current flow according to their resistance values. The higher the resistance, the lower the current for the same voltage source.
 
• Hence, the **current flowing in the circuit** is **0.6 A**, which corresponds to the correct option.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Ohm's Law:**

 
 
• It is a fundamental law of electrical circuits stating the relationship between **current (I)**, **voltage (V)**, and **resistance (R)**: **V = I × R**.
 
• This law is applicable to **linear circuits** where the resistance remains constant regardless of the voltage or current.
 
 
 
• **Series Circuits:**
 
 
• In a series circuit, the total resistance is the **sum of all individual resistances**: **R_total = R1 + R2 + ... + Rn**.
 
• The **current is the same** through all components in a series circuit.
 
• The total voltage is the **sum of the voltages across each component**.
 
 
 
• **Power Dissipation in Resistors:**
 
 
• The power dissipated by a resistor can be calculated using the formula: **P = I² × R**, or **P = V² / R**.
 
• In this circuit, the power dissipated in each resistor would be:
 
 
• For the 15 Ω resistor: **P = (0.6 A)² × 15 Ω = 5.4 W**.
 
• For the 5 Ω resistor: **P = (0.6 A)² × 5 Ω = 1.8 W**.
 
 Total power = **5.4 W + 1.8 W = 7.2 W**.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Series Circuits:**
 
 
• Series circuits are commonly used in **simple electrical systems** where the same current needs to flow through multiple components, such as in **string lights** or **battery packs**.
 
 
 
• **Important Note:** If one component in a series circuit fails (e.g., a resistor burns out), the entire circuit becomes open, and **current stops flowing**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Resistors in Series vs. Parallel:**

 
 
• In a **series connection**, the total resistance increases as resistors are added.
 
• In a **parallel connection**, the total resistance decreases as resistors are added.
 
 
 
• **Units of Measurement:**
 
 
• Resistance is measured in **Ohms (Ω)**.
 
• Voltage is measured in **Volts (V)**.
 
• Current is measured in **Amperes (A)**.
 
 
 
• **Practical Considerations:**
 
 
• In real circuits, factors like **temperature** can affect resistance, causing slight deviations from calculated values.
 
• Resistors have power ratings (in watts) indicating their ability to dissipate heat without damage.
